commentary.bottom_line: Two randomized trials, one in a real deployment in China with 2,113 participants and one simulated in Australia with 592, found that AI literacy education increased health awareness and knowledge and reduced intention to use a chatbot for higher-risk questions. Neither trial measured whether patients went on to question or challenge AI in their own care, so certainty in the practice is low.

perspectives.view: Both studies are randomized, which would start certainty high. Certainty drops for indirectness because the outcomes are awareness, knowledge, and stated intention rather than patient engagement with AI in care. Only one trial used a real deployment, and the Australian trial appears to be a preprint in a simulated setting. The two trials agree in direction.

In the Australian trial, animation and image interventions lowered intention to use ChatGPT for higher-risk scenarios (means 2.42 and 2.69 vs 3.12, p<0.001). This suggests education may steer patients away from unsafe chatbot use. The trial measured intention, not behavior or harm, so it cannot show that errors were caught before reaching patients.

The Chinese trial placed AI literacy e-learning before consultations in a live deployment and reported higher objective health awareness (2.95 vs 2.34, P<0.001) and better consultation quality on secondary outcomes. This suggests a preparatory module can fit into a visit workflow. Completion rates, time burden, and fidelity were not reported in the summary provided.

The larger trial enrolled participants with limited or non-English proficiency, low health literacy, rural residence, older age, and racial or ethnic minority status, and it found benefit. Because the trial ran in China, its results may not transfer directly to Medicaid or US safety-net populations, whose language needs and access to digital education differ.

A UK survey of 120 women at breast clinics found that 80% had no knowledge of AI use there and 37% would trust AI findings. That gap suggests patients often cannot question tools they do not know exist. The Australian trial also found lower trust after education, which may reflect more calibrated judgment rather than loss of confidence in care.

Neither trial summary reports cost, staffing, or content maintenance needs. The Chinese trial used e-learning at scale with 2,113 participants, which suggests a digital format can reach large numbers, but health systems have no cost data from these studies to budget for tool-specific materials.

commentary.research_gap: No trial has measured whether AI literacy education changes what patients do in their own care, such as asking about AI use, declining a tool, or requesting a human reviewer, or whether it reduces harm. Trials in US settings, including Medicaid and safety-net systems, should compare formats, report cost and staff time, and test how long effects last and whether tool-specific education outperforms general AI education.
commentary.underserved_note: The randomized trial in China included participants with limited or non-English proficiency, low health literacy, rural residence, older age, and racial or ethnic minority status, and it found benefit. No test included Medicaid or US safety-net populations, so health systems serving those groups should treat the findings as indirect and evaluate local adaptations.
